newsitem.title: UK: German investors show growing risk appetite -- DMG.
newsitem.headline: German investors show growing risk appetite -- DMG.

text.p: Traditionally conservative German investors are showing an increasing willingness to take risks by buying emerging market debt and picking up their overseas equity investment, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said.
DMG emerging market research head Paul Luke said in a research report Germans had shown a sudden appetite for emerging market risk.

"At present they are devouring emerging market bonds with all the relish of an alderman slurping his soup," he said, adding that developing countries had picked up on this and increased their mark-denominated bond issuance.
In 1996, eastern Europe and Latin America issuers raised $8.1 billion of new money in marks. In 1994, out of $57 billion of emerging market bond issues, $1.6 billion was in marks.

He said the increasing willingness to take risks was also reflected in the success of the Deutsche Telekom issue, leading to a steep rise in Germans invested in stocks, and a surge in the mutual fund sector.
Although the sector is relatively small, the total asset value of funds investing purely in equities rose by 30 percent, with a large slice of this going to non-German markets.
He said a range of demographic and macroeconomic factors were conspiring to turn Germany into a nation of risk takers, at least relative to their reputation as risk avoiders.

For the first time since the Second World War, German individuals have the benefit of inherited wealth, risk assets in Germany are at last beginning to perform relatively well, and the opportunity cost of staying in mark deposits and bonds is high.
"German bond yields are exceptionally low in nominal terms...Like the Japanese they are having to look to equities or to foreign markets for decent returns."

At the same time, Germans are beginning to worry how their retirement will be funded. By 2030, Germany's unfunded pension liabilities will probably rise to around 110 percent of GDP and there will be only two taxpayers per pensioner against about 4.5 presently.
The report also said that Germans may be losing a little of their faith in the mark.

"Notwithstanding the insistence on fairly strong macroeconomic performance from the various countries set to join EMU, the prospect of effective watering down of the mark and the Bundesbank may be making Germans edgy," Luke said.
"In this context, the odds are that the long run trend towards an appreciation of the mark against the dollar may be faltering."
